question: to the Commission Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D) Subject:

Recent investigations, including those by the VRT programme Pano1 and AI Forensics2 reveal that Meta continues to profit from fraudulent advertisements, including scams impersonating public figures and journalists and more than 46 000 health-related advertisements featuring unapproved drugs, deepfakes and false medical claims, viewed 292 million times by EU users since the Digital Services Act (DSA) entered into force. Internal Meta documents reportedly estimate that scam advertisements generate around 10 % of its annual revenue, far exceeding likely fines for non-compliance. On 21 May 2026, the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) and 29 member organisations filed formal complaints with the Commission against Meta over its systematic failure to remove fraudulent financial advertisements. Meanwhile, victims report that national police often lack the resources to investigate such cases, particularly when servers are hosted outside the EU or when the fraud involves less than EUR 5 000. 1.
Is the Commission aware of these findings and has it engaged with Meta on this systemic non-compliance?
Is the Commission considering a formal investigation into Meta under the DSA regarding this issue?

How will the Commission ensure effective follow-up and redress for victims, given that national authorities often cannot act on complaints below certain thresholds or when servers are hosted outside the EU?
https://aiforensics.org/uploads/meta_health.pdf. https://aiforensics.org/uploads/meta_health.pdf.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.9.2026) The Commission takes the concerns raised very seriously. The Commission is aware of the complaints and reports regarding the dissemination of deceptive advertising on Meta’s platforms. In April 2024, the Commission initiated proceedings against the provider of Facebook and Instagram, including in relation to the suspicion that the provider does not comply with obligations related to addressing deceptive advertisements, including financial scam advertisements1. On 24 October 2025, the Commission preliminarily found the provider of Facebook and Instagram in breach of its obligations to put in place user-friendly and easily accessible mechanisms to allow recipients to notify content considered to be illegal and to provide users with an internal complaint-handling system that allows them to effectively challenge content moderation decisions taken by the provider2. The case in relation to financial scam advertisements is ongoing, and the Commission cannot comment on the status of ongoing investigations. Recipients of intermediary services may lodge a complaint against a provider of those services alleging an infringement of the Digital Services Act (DSA)3. Complaints must be submitted to the Digital Services Coordinator (DSC)4 of the Member State where the recipient of the service is located or established. The Commission remains in close contact with competent national authorities through the DSCs to ensure the effective fulfilment of DSA obligations. The revised Victims’ Rights’ Directive5 (June 2026) enhances the rights, protection, and access to justice for victims of crime, including of online frauds. An EU Action Plan on digital frauds and a Strategy on victims’ rights are forthcoming and will contain measures to support victims of online fraud.
